```{r options, include = FALSE}
has_cograph <- requireNamespace("cograph", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6,
                      fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center", dpi = 100)
```

A psychological network is reported as a table of edge weights, but it is read
as a figure. The figure shows at a glance which variables form a cluster,
which variable connects two clusters, and where the negative associations lie.
It can also mislead: the position of the nodes is chosen by a layout
algorithm, edges of very different size can look alike, and colour alone does
not reach every reader. Drawing a network well means encoding the sign and
size of each edge so that they can be read, placing the nodes so that
comparable figures share a layout, and keeping exact values available in the
table that the figure summarizes.

This article draws a Gaussian graphical model of five self-regulated learning
constructs with the `cograph` package, from the default figure to one ready
for publication: layouts, node size and colour, edge encoding and thresholds,
the distribution of edge weights, bootstrap diagnostics, themes, networks of
several groups on a shared layout, and export to a file. The chunks that draw
with `cograph` run only when it is installed.

```{r check, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = !has_cograph}
cat("> `cograph` is not installed, so the cograph plotting chunks below are skipped.")
```

```{r setup}
library(psychnets)
```

## Data

`SRL_GPT` holds 300 sets of responses to the Motivated Strategies for Learning
Questionnaire, each a construct score on a scale from 1 to 7. The responses
were generated by a large language model (GPT) in a study of how such models
answer psychological surveys (Saqr, 2025). A second set, `SRL_Claude`, holds
300 responses generated by another model and is used for the group
comparison.

- **Nodes:** `CSU` (cognitive strategy use), `IV` (intrinsic value), `SE`
  (self-efficacy), `SR` (self-regulation) and `TA` (test anxiety).
- **Observations:** one row per respondent; the data are complete.

`ebic_glasso()` estimates the network: edges are partial correlations selected
by the extended Bayesian information criterion.

```{r fit, eval = has_cograph}
fit <- ebic_glasso(SRL_GPT)
fit
```

The network has 10 edges. Nine are positive, from 0.049 to 0.412, and one,
between self-regulation and test anxiety, is negative (-0.350); the
Gaussian graphical models article interprets them.

## What does the default figure show?

`plot()` on a fitted network draws it with `cograph::splot()`. Each node is a
construct and each edge a partial correlation: the colour of an edge encodes
its sign and the width its absolute size.

```{r default, eval = has_cograph}
plot(fit)
```

The four learning constructs appear as a cluster of wide edges of one colour,
and the edge between self-regulation and test anxiety stands out in the other
colour. Calling `cograph::splot()` directly draws the same figure and accepts
all the arguments used below.

```{r splot-default, eval = has_cograph}
cograph::splot(fit)
```

## Where should the nodes be placed?

The `layout` argument chooses how nodes are placed. A circular layout puts the
nodes on a ring, so their positions are the same in every figure with the same
nodes. A spring layout pulls connected nodes together, so clusters become
visible; `seed` fixes its random start so the figure can be reproduced.

```{r layouts, eval = has_cograph, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 4.5}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(1, 1, 3, 1))
cograph::splot(fit, layout = "circle", title = "circle")
cograph::splot(fit, layout = "spring", seed = 11, title = "spring")
par(op)
```

In the spring layout, cognitive strategy use, self-regulation and intrinsic
value, joined by the widest edges, are drawn close together, and test anxiety
is placed at the margin with its single strong, negative edge. The circle is
the better choice when several networks are compared; the spring layout when
the structure of one network is the point.

## How can nodes carry information?

Node size can show a node property. `scale_nodes_by = "strength"` sizes each
node by its strength, and `node_size_range` sets the
smallest and largest size. The fill, border and label arguments set the
remaining appearance.

```{r nodes, eval = has_cograph}
cograph::splot(
  fit,
  layout = "circle",
  scale_nodes_by = "strength",
  node_size_range = c(4, 12),
  node_fill = c("#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#009E73", "#0072B2", "#CC79A7"),
  node_border_color = "white",
  node_border_width = 2,
  label_size = 0.9,
  title = "Node size scaled by strength"
)
```

For a signed network, `cograph` computes this strength from the signed edge
weights, so the node sizes follow the expected influence of
`net_centralities()` rather than its absolute strength. Cognitive strategy use
(1.198) and intrinsic value (1.001) are drawn largest and test anxiety
(-0.091) smallest. Self-regulation, which has the largest absolute strength
(1.231), is drawn mid-sized because its negative edge with test anxiety
offsets its positive edges (expected influence 0.532). A figure caption that
says "size by strength" should state which of the two is shown.

## How should edges be encoded?

For a signed network, the edge encoding carries the result.
`edge_positive_color` and `edge_negative_color` set the two sign colours, and
`edge_width_range` maps absolute size to width. `threshold` hides edges below
an absolute weight, and `edge_labels` prints each weight, so the sign is
readable from the number as well as from the colour.

```{r edges, eval = has_cograph}
cograph::splot(
  fit,
  layout = "circle",
  threshold = 0.05,
  edge_width_range = c(0.5, 5),
  edge_positive_color = "#0072B2",
  edge_negative_color = "#D55E00",
  edge_labels = TRUE,
  edge_label_size = 0.7,
  edge_label_bg = "white",
  title = "Thresholded edge weights"
)
```

The threshold of 0.05 hides one edge, cognitive strategy use with test anxiety
(0.049), and leaves nine, each labelled with its partial correlation. A
display threshold changes the figure, not the model, and is reported in the
figure caption.

`cograph::plot_edge_weights()` draws the distribution of the edge weights
without a layout.

```{r edge-weights, eval = has_cograph}
cograph::plot_edge_weights(fit)
```

The histogram shows one negative edge (-0.350), four positive edges below 0.2,
three of them the edges of test anxiety, and five edges between 0.2 and 0.41
among the learning constructs; the mean edge weight is 0.17. It is a useful
check on whether a display threshold separates groups of edges or cuts
through one.

## How precise are the edges?

A network figure shows point estimates. Their precision comes from resampling.
`net_boot()` refits the network to bootstrap samples of the respondents and
records the distribution of every edge; `plot()` on the result draws each
edge with its confidence interval. The partial-correlation estimator keeps
this example fast; an applied analysis would use the graphical lasso with at
least 1,000 resamples. The network reliability article covers these
diagnostics in full.

```{r bootstrap, eval = has_cograph, fig.height = 5}
set.seed(1)
bs <- net_boot(SRL_GPT, method = "pcor", n_boot = 250, cores = 1)
bs
plot(bs)
```

Nine of the ten edges have 95% intervals that exclude zero. The exception is
cognitive strategy use with test anxiety, the same small edge that the
threshold above removed. With `type = "edge_diff"`, the plot shows which pairs
of edges differ in size across the bootstrap samples:

```{r edge-diff-box, eval = has_cograph, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 6.5}
plot(bs, type = "edge_diff")
```

`difference_test()` gives the same pairwise comparisons as a table with
confidence intervals, and `style = "forest"` draws each difference with its
interval.

```{r edge-diff-forest, eval = has_cograph, fig.height = 5}
plot(difference_test(bs, type = "edge"), style = "forest")
```

Of the 45 pairs of edges, 26 differ in size. The forest plot shows how large
each difference is, which the box matrix does not.

## How can a figure follow a house style?

The `theme` argument applies a set of colour and style defaults without
changing the model.

```{r themes, eval = has_cograph, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 4.5}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(1, 1, 3, 1))
cograph::splot(fit, theme = "minimal", title = "minimal")
cograph::splot(fit, theme = "colorblind", title = "colorblind")
par(op)
```

The colourblind theme uses colours that remain distinct for readers with the
common forms of colour-vision deficiency; combined with edge labels, the sign
of an edge can be read without colour.

## How can networks of several groups be compared?

`psychnet()` with `group` estimates one network per level of a grouping
column. The example stacks the two response sets and labels each row with its
source.

```{r group-data}
grouped_srl <- rbind(
  data.frame(SRL_GPT, source = "GPT", check.names = FALSE),
  data.frame(SRL_Claude, source = "Claude", check.names = FALSE)
)
```

```{r groups, eval = has_cograph, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 4.5}
group_fit <- psychnet(grouped_srl, group = "source", method = "glasso")
summary(group_fit)
cograph::splot(group_fit, layout = "circle", psych_styling = TRUE)
```

`cograph::splot()` draws the networks as a grid on one layout, so a node has
the same position in every panel and the panels can be compared edge by edge.
Both networks have 10 edges, but the mean absolute edge weight is 0.354 for
the Claude responses against 0.244 for the GPT responses, and the shared
layout makes the differences visible: in the Claude network intrinsic value
and self-efficacy are negatively related, and test anxiety is positively
related to cognitive strategy use and negatively to self-efficacy. A formal
test of the difference requires `net_compare()`.

## How is the figure saved?

The `filename`, `width`, `height` and `res` arguments write the figure to a
file at a chosen size and resolution.

```{r export, eval = FALSE}
cograph::splot(fit, layout = "circle", filename = "network.png",
               width = 8, height = 8, res = 300)
```

## Summary of the arguments

| Task | Arguments |
|---|---|
| Layout | `layout`, `seed`, `layout_scale`, `layout_margin` |
| Nodes | `node_size`, `scale_nodes_by`, `node_size_range`, `node_fill`, `node_shape` |
| Labels | `labels`, `label_size`, `label_color`, `label_position` |
| Edges | `edge_width_range`, `edge_positive_color`, `edge_negative_color`, `edge_alpha` |
| Filtering | `threshold`, `minimum`, `maximum` |
| Edge labels | `edge_labels`, `edge_label_size`, `edge_label_bg`, `edge_label_style` |
| Themes | `theme`, `background`, `title` |
| Export | `filename`, `width`, `height`, `res` |

A network figure is read alongside its edge table: the figure shows the
structure, the table gives the values, and a fixed layout makes figures of
different groups comparable.

## References

Saqr, M. (2025). Delving into the psychology of machines: Exploring the structure of self-regulated learning via LLM-generated survey responses. *Computers in Human Behavior*, 173, 108769. [doi:10.1016/j.chb.2025.108769](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chb.2025.108769)
